prompt: Who reads an error page?

choices.text: Only the support team, through the monitoring dashboard
choices.why: The team reads the log; the page goes to whoever asked.

choices.text: Whoever sent the request
choices.why: Right. That may be a patient, a script or a stranger.

choices.text: Only signed-in patients
choices.why: Errors happen before and without sign-in too.

choices.text: Nobody; browsers hide them
choices.why: Browsers show them, and scripts read them.

prompt: Why is a traceback on an error page a problem, if each fact in it is small?

choices.text: Tracebacks slow the page down
choices.why: Speed is not the issue.

choices.text: Together they show how the application is built
choices.why: Right. Paths, versions and code save a stranger hours of guessing.

choices.text: Patients complain about the colours
choices.why: Not the concern.

choices.text: Python forbids printing tracebacks over HTTP
choices.why: Python allowed it, which is how it happened.

prompt: The log is private. Why does the lesson still call it 'not a safe'?

choices.text: Logs are deleted every night
choices.why: Most are kept for months.

choices.text: Logs are always public on the internet
choices.why: They are not public, just widely read.

choices.text: More people read it than anybody remembers
choices.why: Right. The log service, its backups, and the tickets lines get pasted into.

choices.text: Logs cannot hold tracebacks
choices.why: They can, and should.

prompt: Match each item to where it belongs.
How many of the four tests failed against the first version?
What did the old server's log hold after lucia signed in?

choices.text: Nothing about the sign-in
choices.why: It wrote a line with every field.

choices.text: A hash of her password
choices.why: Not even that: the plain text.

choices.text: Her password, in plain text
choices.why: Right. Beside her name, for every reader of the log.

choices.text: Only her name and the time
choices.why: That is what the fix logs.

prompt: What does pytest's `caplog` fixture give a test?

choices.text: What was logged while the test ran
choices.why: Right. The tests read it to check what the log holds.

choices.text: The server's log file from disk
choices.why: It captures records in memory; no file is read.

choices.text: A copy of the HTTP response
choices.why: That is the test client's job.

choices.text: The traceback of the failing test
choices.why: pytest prints that itself.

prompt: Why did the test for a password in the log need `caplog.set_level(logging.INFO, logger="portal")`?

choices.text: To hide the password from pytest's output
choices.why: It reveals more, not less.

choices.text: INFO is the only level Flask writes
choices.why: Flask writes several levels.

choices.text: Without it the INFO line is not captured, so the test cannot see it
choices.why: Right. A test that cannot see the line passes for the wrong reason.

choices.text: Because the portal logger is disabled by default
choices.why: It is not disabled; the capture level was the issue.

prompt: What does a patient see when the fixed portal fails?

choices.text: The traceback, shortened to the last line
choices.why: Even the last line names the code.

choices.text: A sentence and a reference
choices.why: Right. Enough to act on, and to quote to the clinic.

choices.text: A blank page
choices.why: A blank page tells nobody anything, including what to do.

choices.text: Flask's debugger
choices.why: That is for a developer's own machine.

prompt: Why is the reference drawn from `secrets` and different every time?

choices.text: To make it harder for the team to find
choices.why: The team finds it by searching the log.

choices.text: Because a counter would be slower
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: It identifies one failure and says nothing else
choices.why: Right. A counter would tell a stranger how many errors the portal has had.

choices.text: The log refuses repeated values
choices.why: Logs accept anything.

prompt: The fixed handler writes the traceback to the log with `log.___("unexpected error ref=%s …")`.
How is Flask's debug mode switched on, according to the lesson?

choices.text: By app.run(debug=True) in the code that ships
choices.why: That is the way it must never be switched on.

choices.text: By --debug or FLASK_DEBUG=1, on your machine
choices.why: Right. Never by code that ships.

choices.text: It is always on in Flask 3
choices.why: It is off by default.

choices.text: By a setting in the browser
choices.why: The server decides.

prompt: Put what happens, when the fixed portal meets an unexpected error, in order.
items: the handler draws a random reference
the traceback is logged with that reference
the patient receives a sentence and the reference
the team searches the log for the reference

prompt: Which of these never go in a log? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: a wrong password
choices.why: Often the right one for another site, or one typo away.

choices.text: a session id
choices.why: Reading it lets somebody act as that session.

choices.text: an exam result
choices.why: Health data; log the record's identifier instead.

choices.text: that a sign-in failed, and for whom
choices.why: That is exactly what to log.

prompt: A name with a line break in it was logged with `%s`. What went wrong?

choices.text: One attempt became two lines in the log
choices.why: Right. The second line starts with text the sender chose.

choices.text: The log refused to write the name
choices.why: It wrote it, as it arrived.

choices.text: The password was logged too
choices.why: That was a separate line of the old code.

choices.text: Python crashed on the newline
choices.why: Python logged it without complaint.

prompt: What does `%r` do for a name in a log line?

choices.text: Removes the line breaks and the quotes
choices.why: It keeps them, visible and escaped.

choices.text: Encrypts the name
choices.why: It encodes, it does not encrypt.

choices.text: Writes it as a Python literal, \n escaped
choices.why: Right. The line break stays visible and inside one line.

choices.text: Replaces it with the account number
choices.why: It writes the name, encoded.

prompt: Why log a record's identifier rather than a patient's full details?

choices.text: Identifiers are shorter, so logs are smaller
choices.why: Size is a side effect, not the reason.

choices.text: Each copy of personal data is one more place an erasure must reach
choices.why: Right. The identifier lets the team look the record up, with authorisation.

choices.text: Log services refuse names
choices.why: They accept anything.

choices.text: Identifiers are encrypted by default
choices.why: They are plain values.

prompt: Health data is the most protected category of personal data under Brazil's law, the ___.
Match each event to why it is worth a log line.

pairs.left: many failed sign-ins for one account

pairs.right: who may do what changed, and by whom

prompt: Put the five things a security log line carries in the lesson's order.
Lesson 1's 404 for somebody else's booking: why log it?

choices.text: To show the patient later
choices.why: Logs are for the team.

choices.text: Because every 404 must be logged
choices.why: Not every one; refusals of access are the point.

choices.text: One is a mistake; fifty are a pattern
choices.why: Right. Refusals counted over time show somebody trying.

choices.text: To fix the 404 automatically
choices.why: Nothing to fix: the refusal was right.

prompt: A team logs every security event perfectly and nobody reads the logs. What does the lesson say?

choices.text: That is enough for compliance
choices.why: The lesson is about protection, not paperwork.

choices.text: It protects nothing: at least alert on rare events
choices.why: Right. Many failed sign-ins, a role change at night, a spike in refusals.

choices.text: Logs should then be switched off to save space
choices.why: Then the record would be missing when it is needed.

choices.text: The application should read its own logs
choices.why: Watching belongs to people and tools outside the code.

prompt: A developer adds `log.debug("request %s", request.headers)` to chase a bug. Which row of the never-log table does it break?

choices.text: Full card numbers
choices.why: Headers do not carry card numbers.

choices.text: Session ids and tokens: the Cookie header carries them
choices.why: Right. Every request's session would be in the log.

choices.text: None: headers are metadata
choices.why: Some metadata is a credential.

choices.text: Clinical notes
choices.why: Those travel in bodies, not headers.

prompt: A support agent asks to see the traceback on the page again, 'just for a week'. What do you offer?

choices.text: Turn it on for staff browsers only
choices.why: The page cannot tell who is staff from the browser.

choices.text: Turn on the debugger for a week
choices.why: That is worse than the traceback.

choices.text: Search the log by the reference the patient reads out
choices.why: Right. Every fact they want is there already.

choices.text: Email them every traceback
choices.why: One more copy in one more inbox.

prompt: Which lines would the fixed portal write for a failed sign-in? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: the level WARNING
choices.why: log.warning is used for a failure.

choices.text: the name, as a quoted literal
choices.why: Written with %r.

choices.text: the password that was typed
choices.why: Never.

choices.text: the session cookie
choices.why: Never.
